newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans villagers attack Hutu refugee camps.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans villagers attack Hutu refugee camps.

text.p: Zairean villagers armed with machetes attacked Rwandan refugee camps in eastern Zaire on Tuesday to avenge the killing of six Zaireans, witnesses said.
They said residents of Kasese village 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani city left at dawn for two nearby camps for 55,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees to take revenge and shooting followed.
"This morning at 6 a.m. the villagers decided to go and take revenge and make the refugees flee. They took machetes," said Samy Janga, a Kasese schoolteacher.
"Soon afterwards we heard shooting which went on for an hour and a half. Some villagers ran into the forest to hide," he added. Travellers said it was impossible to pass Kasese because of fighting.
Six Zaireans were killed and two wounded at Kasese on Monday in an attack blamed on Hutu extremists by villagers, who stopped aid workers reaching the camp and looted the same day.
But one survivor of the attack told Reuters she was shot by men who bore the hallmarks of ethnic Tutsi Alliance troops and witnesses said the attackers were uniformed.

"The soldiers wore uniform. They were tall and thin and I heard them speaking Kinyarwanda. They were not refugees," said Mayaza Apaijoma, 20, being treated at Kabonda Catholic hospital after being shot in the thigh.
A two-year old girl, shot in the stomach, was also being treated at the hospital.
The testimony is the latest in a series of signs of a concerted attempt to destabilize a repatriation programme by Alliance troops fearful of the presence of armed Hutu militants among the refugees.

Zaireans said they looted aid vehicles on Monday at the urging of Tutsi-dominated rebels, who have seized half of Africa's third largest country since October in a war to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Meanwhile officials from Rwanda, the rebel Alliance and the U.N. refugee agency arrived in Kisangani on Tuesday for talks under the Tripartite Commission on Repatriation.
"We are here to resolve these (repatriation) problems. The refugees should go using any means -- by air, river or road," said Ephraim Kabaija, Head of Rwanda's Commission for Repatriation.
Aid work was suspended for a second consecutive day on Tuesday but aid agencies said they would try to contact camps for a total of nearly 90,000 refugees including the 55,000 at Kasese.

In addition to the 55,000 at Kasese, 32,000 are at a makeshift camp at Biaro, 42 km (25 miles) south of the city. UNHCR chief Sadako Ogata said on Monday a rebel operation near Kasese camp that day following the reported killings of the six Zaireans had raised fears of a new refugee exodus.
The governor of Zaire's Eastern province, appointed with rebel blessing, said on Sunday a U.N. airlift for the refugees should not start until May 5 because of a cholera epidemic.
But in Geneva, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said the cholera outbreak was not big enough to be classed an epidemic.
"If it was an epidemic we would be seeing thousands of cases and not the numbers that we have already," said Lianne Kuppens, a medical officer with WHO's cholera task force, on Tuesday.
"Our latest figures say there have been 170 confirmed cases and nine deaths," she told Reuters by telephone. "I would not say that it is an epidemic, I would say it is an outbreak."

Leonard Kinuani, the WHO representative in Kisangani, declared the epidemic on April 13. WHO headquarters has not clarified the status of Kinuani, a Zairean, or whether he was authorised to declare a cholera epidemic unilaterally.
The refugees are the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
The refugees have fled 600 km (375 miles) since last October to avoid the rebels, who are supported by Rwanda's government.
